title: The Princess Who Wrote History
subtitle: Gulbadan Begum and the Memory of an Empire
region: Kabul, Agra, Fatehpur Sikri and the Hajj route
moral: History grows wiser when more voices are allowed to speak.

sources.citation: Gulbadan Begum, The History of Humayun (Humayun-Nama), trans. A.S. Beveridge, Royal Asiatic Society, 1902
sources.note: Primary memoir, surviving in a single incomplete Persian manuscript.

sources.citation: British Library, Add MS 24063, Humayun-Nama manuscript record
sources.note: Physical manuscript basis for Gulbadan's text.

sources.citation: Ruby Lal, Vagabond Princess: The Great Adventures of Gulbadan, Yale University Press, 2021
sources.note: Recent reassessment of Gulbadan as an author and traveller, not merely a source for Humayun.

panels.shot: slow three-quarter view, medium close-up, with architectural backdrop

dialogue.text: In Akbar’s marble halls, one woman of Babur’s blood sharpened her reed pen and quietly set an empire’s memory to paper.

panels.shot: wide interior establishing shot, slightly high angle

dialogue.text: By the late 1580s, Fatehpur Sikri rang with arguments of scholars and the marching feet of soldiers, but in one quiet women’s apartment, a princess turned the past over in her hands like a string of beads.

panels.shot: medium shot, low angle to give subtle prominence

dialogue.text: Gulbadan Begum, daughter of Babur, half-sister of Humayun, aunt of Akbar, had seen Kabul’s mountain winds and the dust of Indian plains. Now, her nephew asked her to write of those days.

panels.shot: tight close-up on Gulbadan’s face, eyes distant

dialogue.speaker: gulbadan_begum
dialogue.text: How many lives lie between my father’s tents and this stone city?

panels.shot: soft-edged memory tableau, wide landscape shot

dialogue.text: Her earliest memories were not marble pavilions but the rough camps of Babur’s household, women and children moving with the army, their lives tied to a line of kings chasing fortune across Kabul and Hindustan.

panels.shot: medium shot, interior memory of the haram, eye-level

dialogue.text: As Humayun took Babur’s place, Gulbadan grew into one of the senior women of the dynasty, watching brothers, cousins and rivals move in and out of favour, alliance and exile.

panels.shot: wide shot of a courtyard, slightly elevated angle

dialogue.text: She saw the empire crumble under Humayun, heard of his hurried flights and uneasy shelters. For the women, defeat meant new journeys, uncertain loyalties, and the careful keeping of kin in dangerous times.

panels.shot: medium shot, dimly lit interior, candlelight

dialogue.text: She lived through the dizzy swing of fortune: Humayun’s return to power, his fall from the library steps in Delhi, the child Akbar’s narrow escapes and coronation on a dusty platform far from any city.

panels.shot: medium shot, intimate interior of Akbar’s courtly audience with women, side angle

dialogue.text: Under Akbar, Gulbadan became more than a shadow of the past. As senior aunt she advised, negotiated marriages, and represented a living bridge to Babur and Humayun in a court hungry for its own origin story.

panels.shot: medium close-up on Gulbadan presenting a petition-like scroll, three-quarter view

dialogue.text: When she and other royal women sought permission for the Hajj, their voices carried weight. Through petitions and quiet insistence, they argued for a journey many deemed too perilous for the haram.

panels.shot: epic wide shot of caravan on the move, slightly low angle

dialogue.text: In 1575, Gulbadan led an imperial caravan towards the sea, bound for the Hajj. For seven years she and other women of the dynasty traveled, prayed and negotiated the long route between Hindustan and the Holy Cities.

panels.shot: wide shot of a coastal port, bird’s-eye angle

dialogue.text: They crossed seas from an Indian port toward Arabia, part pilgrims, part diplomats, their presence weaving Mughal authority into the wider currents of Indian Ocean trade, Ottoman power and sacred travel.

panels.shot: medium wide shot of a camp near the Haramain, twilight

dialogue.text: In and around the Holy Places, Gulbadan’s life braided devotion with politics: receiving envoys, managing finances, responding to news from Akbar’s court, and preserving the dignity of Mughal women far from home.

panels.shot: medium shot on ship’s deck, horizon level

dialogue.text: By the early 1580s she returned, seasoned by years of movement, storms and negotiations. The journey itself would leave only scattered traces, but it had sharpened her eye for how fragile power and safety could be.

panels.shot: medium interior shot, low angle behind her shoulder, focusing on page

dialogue.text: When Akbar called for histories of his house, Gulbadan answered not as an ornament but as an author. She set herself to write the Humayun-Nama, a woman’s view onto the storms of a man’s reign.

panels.shot: tight shot on her hand and pen, extreme close-up

dialogue.text: She wrote in Persian of quarrels in the haram, of brothers’ divisions, of everyday routines and sudden disasters, anchoring grand events in small, observed moments rather than in the flattery expected of courtly chronicles.

panels.shot: medium shot, two female attendants nearby, side angle

dialogue.text: Sometimes she wrote with her own hand, sometimes she dictated. In either case, the choices of what to tell and how to tell it were hers, shaped by loyalty to Humayun and by a clear memory of his failings.

panels.shot: memory montage, soft focus, medium-wide interior

dialogue.text: Her narrative did not stride like an official victory scroll. It moved between private rooms and public decisions, between letters and journeys, letting readers feel how imperial choices rippled through the lives of wives, sisters and daughters.

panels.shot: medium shot, contemplative, window light on her face

dialogue.text: She wrote within the bounds of family loyalty, sometimes veiling conflict, sometimes hinting at it. Even in what she left unsaid, her careful omissions reveal how a woman at court navigated truth, discretion and authority.

panels.shot: wide shot of an imperial library room, slightly high angle

dialogue.text: Her work joined the growing pile of histories ordered by Akbar, but it was unlike the others—a first-person record by a Mughal woman, preserving not only battles and treaties but the textures of a shared household past.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot of a single manuscript on a table, lamp-lit, overhead angle

dialogue.text: Only one incomplete manuscript of her Humayun-Nama survives, carried far from the court to a distant library. Yet in those surviving pages, Gulbadan Begum’s voice still widens our understanding of empire, family and who may write history.
